title: Why Jason Cohen finally called bullshit on a spammy guest-post offer
summary: Jason Cohen reflects on why he answers spam and pandering offers politely: fear of offending famous or soon-to-be-famous people. He asks when a blogger earns the right to say what they think and argues that social-media "honesty" is mostly performance. Reflective and personal, light on tactics.

principles.text: Politeness toward bad offers is often fear of offending influential people, not real courtesy.
principles.quote: I'm afraid I might piss off someone famous or potentially famous who then might not want to work with me in future or even say something bad about me in public.

principles.text: Don't hand your audience's channel to anonymous affiliate marketers pushing products under the guise of content.
principles.quote: these people are affiliate marketers, and what they neglected to mention in the introductory email is that these auto-published articles would furthermore push products for them to monetize.

principles.text: Saying what you honestly feel, even if it annoys someone, is a milestone worth reaching.
principles.quote: I finally grew the stones to say what I feel even if it pisses someone off.

principles.text: Most social media 'authenticity' is performance: bloggers project more confidence and certainty than they have.
principles.quote: Bloggers fluff their feathers, coming off more confident, smarter, and more sure than they are

principles.text: Pandering to minor celebrities for reciprocity undermines honest engagement.
principles.quote: Twitterers RT and "follow" and pander to the most minor of celebs

principles.text: You don't need to earn the right to disagree with respected people; waiting for an audience size threshold is a trap.
principles.quote: When do I earn the right to say what I think? Why do I think I need to "earn" that right?
